questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13932638/assets/3687e362fea73defca43332ee70f232282ad1eded9dc14cbbc045de4324067f0.png)

The point $P$ is located on the unit circle, as shown above. The $y$-coordinate of $P$ is $-\frac{6}{7}.$ What is the $x$-coordinate of $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the point $P$ lies on the unit circle, it must satisfy the Pythagorean theorem: 

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1
$$

Substituting $y=-\frac{6}{7}$ into the above and solving for $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{(-\frac{6}{7})}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+(\frac{36}{49}) & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1-\frac{36}{49} \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{13}{49} \\ x & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{13}{49}} \\ x & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{13}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we select the positive answer since $x$ is positive in the fourth quadrant. So our final answer is $x=\frac{\sqrt{13}}{7}.$

questions.problem: If $cos⁡\theta =-\frac{1}{4}$ and $\frac{\pi }{2}<\theta <\pi $ then what is the value of $sin⁡\theta ?$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13932638/assets/7e887638bb8b3b135c6a8e6eecf564fe8310a43f2ce26f8b565ec6966bafb89c.png)

We're given that $cos⁡\theta =-\frac{1}{4}.$ We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $sin⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $cos⁡\theta =-\frac{1}{4}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{1}{4})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{1}{16}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{15}{16}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{15}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $sin⁡\theta $ is positive in the second quadrant. So, $sin⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{15}}{4}.$

questions.problem: If $sin⁡\theta =\frac{7}{8}$ and $\frac{\pi }{2}<\theta <\pi $ then what is the value of $sec⁡\theta ?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's sketch our angle $\theta $ in the coordinate plane.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13932638/assets/5c98414bbe0e1e373864e9ec1d6b8667bb0032c8824f20bed1e6f9b9079c4d02.png)

We're given that $sin⁡\theta =\frac{7}{8}.$ We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $cos⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $sin⁡\theta =\frac{7}{8}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{7}{8})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{49}{64}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{15}{64}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{15}}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $cos⁡\theta $ is negative in the second quadrant. So, $cos⁡\theta =-\frac{\sqrt{15}}{8}.$

Finally, knowing that $sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{cos⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{(-\frac{\sqrt{15}}{8})}=-\frac{8}{\sqrt{15}}=-\frac{8\sqrt{15}}{15}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Applying the Pythagorean Theorem to the Unit Circle
canonical_examples.problem:
The point $P$ is located in the second quadrant and lies on the unit circle. 
The $y$-coordinate of $P$ is $\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}.$ What is the $x$-coordinate of $P?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since the point $P$ lies on the unit circle, it must satisfy the Pythagorean theorem: 

$$
x^2+y^2=1 .
$$

Substituting $y=\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}$ into the above and solving for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1-\frac{1}{2} \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ x & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} \\ x & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we select the negative answer since $x$ is negative in the second quadrant. Therefore, $x = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\cos\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sin\theta = -\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{3}{4}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\pm \frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $\cos\theta$ is positive in the fourth quadrant. So, $\cos\theta = \dfrac 1 2.$

Finally, knowing that $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta},$ we have

$$
\tan\theta = \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)} =-\sqrt 3.
$$

$$
\cos\theta = -\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\sin\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{3}{4}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\pm \frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $\sin\theta$ is negative in the third quadrant. So, $\sin\theta = -\dfrac 1 2.$

Finally, knowing that $\csc\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta},$ we have

$$
